rv.q: The production feels undernourished, lacking the muscular intensity and emotional depth that might have made this a more compelling evening.

Lyle Kessler’s harrowing play, about two imperfectly socialized brothers living like feral animals in a rundown neighborhood of North Philadelphia, acquires unexpected emotional nuance under Daniel Sullivan’s incisive helming.

If these words are not too strange to use about a very dark power play about feral brothers and a violent kidnapping, "Orphans" is a giddy delight -- an acting treat, a fast-talking adrenaline jolt and lots of fun.
In the end what we remember is Sturridge’s astonishing turn.
Or, really, anything better than Orphans.
This is a play more fun to act in than watch.
It's become a dismayingly rare pleasure to see a serious play on Broadway, and while this revival, like "Orphans" itself, is far from perfect, it's still very much worth seeing.
The production is hampered by Baldwin's miscasting and a play that feels more like an acting exercise than a fully realized drama.
That’s about it for kicks of color in this dispiritingly pallid show.

Director Daniel Sullivan makes the fatal mistake of trusting a play that is just an excuse for actors to fling themselves around a squalid set and out-emote each other. The airy, far-too-clean space only shows up Orphans' contrivances. Foster and Sturridge are both commendable-physically robust, emo...
It's a shame that it took 30 years to bring this briskly entertaining, deeply affecting play to Broadway; but at least Orphans has arrived in good hands.
They make this simple story feel both real and somehow larger than life.
The production is blessed with three strong performances that make the most of Kessler's dialogue and the complex relationships between these damaged men.
Although the unusual scenario that it explores is engaging at first, it eventually runs out of steam and inspiration.
“Orphans” remains as synthetic as ever, only now Tom Sturridge, Ben Foster, and Alec Baldwin do the bravura thesping.
Without a menacing atmosphere, "Orphans" -- with its hermetically sealed environment and elliptical story-telling -- now plays like cut-rate Pinter.
In its Broadway premiere, we get to see some of those thespian fireworks, but the full impact of Kessler’s shattering tale of little boys lost is lost amid the craving for audience affection.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this Lyle Kessler revival, with many finding the play derivative and dated despite strong performances. Baldwin and the cast earn praise, but the material itself is often dismissed as "sub-Pinter" that fails to transcend its 1980s origins.

sg.ra: Shubert/SeatPlan place rows C-E as 'just right' — close enough to catch facial detail without the stage-height skew that rows AA/A suffer inside this shallow 26'9" proscenium house; TickPick singles out row B (seats 105-110) as the best seat in the Schoenfeld.

SeatPlan notes the mezzanine overhang starts at row J but only begins clipping the top of the stage at row Q — so K-P sits in the narrow band that's still unobstructed yet priced below premium; TickPick and Headout independently flag K-P as the value pocket in this 1,079-seat Shubert house.

sg.vl: Overhang cuts the top of the stage
sg.ra: SeatPlan explicitly says rows beyond Q lose the top of the stage to the mezzanine overhang, and Headout/TickPick corroborate that under-overhang seats 'might have obstructed views from the overhang of the box seats or the mezzanine itself' — a real issue in this shallow Shubert house where the mezz projects forward.

sg.vl: Overhead sweep of the whole stage
sg.ra: SeatPlan and TickPick both cite front center mezz rows A-B as offering 'excellent overhead views perfect for appreciating the stage in one sweep' — the Schoenfeld's mezz hangs closer to the stage than larger Shubert houses, so row A feels surprisingly close rather than distant.

SeatPlan flags E-G as benefiting from 'great rake for aerial views which cover the entire stage below' — the Schoenfeld mezz is steeper than most Shubert houses, so E-G keeps the full stage visible where a flatter rake would start clipping; Headout calls it a value tier below the premium A-D band.

Multiple sources describe rear mezz past row F as 'a gamble... actors start to look like LEGO figures' — despite the Schoenfeld only having 392 mezz seats, the steep rake trades sightline for proximity and you lose emotional read on faces; a J104 reviewer conceded 'nearly center, no obstructions' but 2nd-to-last row.

SeatPlan notes 'single-digit seats in rows A-D' of the side mezz 'are more directly above the stage and feel surprisingly close' — the Schoenfeld's narrow 40-foot proscenium means side-mezz angles are less punishing than wider houses, though TickPick warns the far edges of rows 'have slightly blocked views of the corners of the stage'.
